title: Arılar ve gıda güvenliği
text: Bees play a crucial role in food production because they pollinate many of the crops we eat. In recent decades, however, bee populations have declined sharply in many parts of the world. Scientists attribute this decline to several factors, including pesticides, habitat loss and disease. The consequences could be substantial: without bees, the price of fruit and vegetables would rise, and some foods might become scarce. To prevent further losses, several countries have restricted the use of certain pesticides and encouraged farmers to plant wild flowers along the edges of their fields.

title: Uyku ve hafıza
text: Sleep is not simply a period of rest. During sleep, the brain processes information collected during the day and transfers important memories into long-term storage. Several studies indicate that students who sleep well after learning retain information better than those who stay awake. Lack of sleep, in contrast, can impair concentration and reduce the ability to solve problems. Although many students believe that studying late into the night will enhance their results, researchers emphasise that a regular sleep pattern is essential for effective learning.

title: Şehirlerde ısı adaları
text: Cities are often several degrees warmer than the surrounding countryside, a phenomenon known as the urban heat island effect. Concrete and asphalt absorb heat during the day and release it slowly at night, while the lack of vegetation reduces natural cooling. As global temperatures rise, this effect is likely to become more dangerous, especially for elderly residents. Some cities are trying to mitigate the problem by planting trees, creating green roofs and using light-coloured materials that reflect sunlight. These measures are relatively cheap and can also improve air quality.

title: Çevrimiçi öğrenme
text: Online learning has expanded rapidly in recent years, and the pandemic accelerated this trend. Supporters argue that online courses provide flexible access to education for people who cannot attend traditional classes. Critics, on the other hand, point out that many students struggle to stay motivated without regular face-to-face contact. Research suggests that the most effective approach combines online materials with some classroom teaching. Such “blended” courses appear to retain the flexibility of online learning while maintaining the social benefits of the classroom.

title: Antibiyotik direnci
text: Antibiotics are among the most important discoveries in modern medicine. However, their excessive use has contributed to the emergence of bacteria that no longer respond to treatment. When antibiotics are used unnecessarily or incorrectly, the most resistant bacteria can survive and multiply. Health experts warn that antibiotic resistance could make common infections deadly again. To tackle this threat, doctors are urged to prescribe antibiotics only when necessary, and researchers are trying to develop new drugs that bacteria cannot easily resist.

title: Dil öğrenmede yaş
text: It is widely assumed that children learn foreign languages more easily than adults. Research partly supports this view: young children are better at acquiring a native-like accent. However, adults often make faster progress at the beginning because they can use their knowledge of grammar and learning strategies. The age at which learning begins is therefore only one factor among many. Motivation, the amount of exposure to the language and the quality of teaching appear to be equally important in determining success.

title: Plastik kirliliği
text: Every year, large amounts of plastic waste enter the oceans. Much of it breaks down into tiny pieces called microplastics, which are consumed by fish and other marine animals. Scientists are still investigating the long-term effects of microplastics on human health, but early studies indicate that they may be harmful. Several countries have banned single-use plastic bags, and some companies have adopted packaging made from renewable materials. Experts argue, however, that such measures will be insufficient unless the overall production of plastic is reduced.

title: Kentleşme ve göç
text: In recent decades, large numbers of people have migrated from rural areas to cities in search of employment. This movement has brought about rapid economic growth in many developing countries. At the same time, it has given rise to serious problems, such as overcrowded housing, traffic congestion and pressure on public services. Governments have responded in different ways. Some have invested in infrastructure in smaller towns to reduce the flow of people to the capital, whereas others have focused on building affordable housing in existing cities.

title: Yenilenebilir enerji
text: The cost of solar and wind power has fallen dramatically in recent years. In many regions, renewable energy can now compete on price with electricity from coal or gas. Nevertheless, several obstacles remain. Because the sun does not always shine and the wind does not always blow, energy must be stored for later use, and current battery technology is still expensive. Furthermore, existing power grids were designed for large central power stations rather than many small producers. Experts estimate that a substantial amount of investment will be required to modernise them.

title: Sosyal medya ve gençler
text: Social media is an essential part of daily life for most teenagers. It allows them to maintain friendships and explore their interests. However, a growing body of evidence suggests that excessive use may be linked to anxiety and poor sleep. The relationship is complex: it is not clear whether social media causes these problems or whether anxious teenagers simply spend more time online. Researchers therefore warn against simple conclusions and recommend that parents focus on how their children use social media rather than only on how long they use it.

title: Kahve ve sağlık
text: For many years, coffee was regarded as an unhealthy habit. Recent research, however, has challenged this widely held view. Large studies indicate that moderate coffee drinkers may have a lower risk of certain long-term diseases. Some scientists attribute these benefits to natural compounds found in coffee beans. Nevertheless, they emphasise that the findings do not prove that coffee itself prevents disease, since coffee drinkers may differ from non-drinkers in other ways, such as diet and income.

title: Yaşlanan nüfus
text: In many developed countries, the proportion of older people is rising steadily, while birth rates remain low. This demographic shift poses a significant challenge for governments. As the number of retired people increases, fewer workers are available to pay the taxes that fund pensions and health care. Some countries have responded by raising the retirement age; others encourage immigration to address labour shortages. Economists argue that a combination of policies, including investment in technology, will be required to sustain economic growth.

title: Çanak çömlekteki besin izleri
text: For many years, archaeologists studied ancient pots mainly for their shapes and decorations. Today, however, scientists can also examine the tiny traces of food left inside them. Using chemical tests, they can identify fats, oils and even milk in pieces of pottery that are thousands of years old. This method has revealed that some early farming communities in Europe were already producing cheese in prehistoric times. Such findings provide valuable evidence about what people ate and how they prepared their meals. They also show that a simple broken pot can contain a surprising amount of information about the past.

title: Ötegezegenlerin izinde
text: Planets outside our solar system are called exoplanets. Because they are very far away and much smaller than their stars, they are difficult to observe directly. Astronomers therefore use a clever method. When a planet passes in front of its star, the star's light becomes slightly weaker for a short time. Telescopes can detect this small change in brightness. By measuring how much the light drops, scientists can estimate the size of the planet. Using this approach, space missions have identified a large number of exoplanets. A few of them may even have conditions similar to those on Earth.

title: Dikey tarım
text: Vertical farming is a method of growing crops inside tall buildings instead of open fields. Plants are placed on shelves stacked one above another, and they receive light from special lamps rather than the sun. Because water is recycled within the system, vertical farms require far less water than traditional farms. They can also be built in urban areas, so fresh vegetables travel only short distances to shops. However, these farms use a significant amount of electricity, which makes them expensive to run. For this reason, experts consider them a useful addition to traditional agriculture rather than a complete substitute for it.

title: Sınav öncesi yazmanın gücü
text: Many students feel nervous before an important exam, and this anxiety can affect their performance. In one study conducted by psychologists, a group of students was asked to write freely about their worries for a few minutes just before a test. Another group simply sat quietly. The students who wrote about their feelings achieved higher scores than those who did not. The researchers suggest that writing helps people to clear their minds. When worries are put on paper, they take up less mental space, which enables students to focus on the questions. This relatively simple technique costs nothing and can be used by almost anyone.

title: Mikrokredi
text: Microcredit is a system that provides very small loans to people who cannot borrow money from ordinary banks. Most of these borrowers live in poverty and have no property to offer as security. With a small loan, a person can buy a sewing machine, a few animals or goods to sell at a market. In this way, they can start a small business and earn a regular income. Supporters argue that microcredit has helped many families, especially women, to become more independent. However, critics point out that some borrowers fall into debt when interest rates are too high.

title: İpek Yolu'nda fikir alışverişi
text: The Silk Road is often remembered as a route along which luxury goods such as silk and spices were carried between China and the Mediterranean. Yet historians today note that the network, which was used for many centuries, also enabled the exchange of ideas and technologies. Papermaking, which was developed in China, gradually spread westward and eventually reached the Islamic world. Religions, medical knowledge and artistic styles travelled in a similar way, carried by merchants, pilgrims and scholars. Diseases were transmitted as well, and the plague that devastated medieval Europe is believed to have moved partly along these trade routes. Thus, the Silk Road connected distant societies in ways that were both beneficial and destructive.

title: Ahtapotların zekâsı
text: Octopuses are widely regarded as the most intelligent invertebrates. Unlike humans, whose neurons are concentrated largely in the brain, an octopus has the majority of its neurons located in its eight arms. As a result, each arm can respond to touch and taste on its own, without waiting for instructions from the brain. Laboratory studies have demonstrated that octopuses can open jars, find their way through mazes and even tell individual people apart. What makes this ability remarkable is that octopuses have short lives and receive no care from their parents after hatching. Consequently, scientists believe that much of their behaviour must be acquired rapidly through direct experience rather than passed on from older generations.

title: Emojiler ve yanlış anlaşılma
text: Emojis were originally designed to add emotional tone to short text messages, which often lack the facial expressions and voice cues present in face-to-face conversation. However, research suggests that these small images are not always interpreted in the same way. People who are shown the same emoji often rate its meaning very differently, and the disagreement is even greater when the image appears on different devices, with each company drawing its emojis in a slightly different style. A smiling face that looks friendly on one phone may appear sarcastic on another. Cultural background also plays a role; a gesture regarded as positive in one country may be considered rude elsewhere. In short, emojis may cause confusion as easily as they prevent it.

title: Açık etiketli plasebo
text: The placebo effect, in which patients feel better after receiving a treatment that contains no active ingredient, has long been thought to depend on deception. It was believed that the pill would only work if patients thought it was real medicine. Recent studies, however, have questioned this belief. In several trials with people suffering from chronic pain, some participants were openly told that they were taking sugar pills. Surprisingly, many of them still reported a significant reduction in pain compared with those who received no pills at all. Researchers suggest that the ritual of taking a pill regularly may trigger the body's own pain-relieving mechanisms. Although these findings are promising, scientists warn that placebos cannot cure serious diseases.

title: Jeotermal enerji
text: Geothermal energy is heat that comes from deep inside the Earth. In regions where hot rocks lie relatively close to the surface, such as Iceland, underground water is heated by the rocks and brought to the surface as steam, which is then used to drive turbines and generate electricity. Unlike solar and wind power, geothermal plants can operate day and night regardless of the weather, so they provide a steady supply of energy. Nevertheless, their use remains limited. Suitable sites are found mainly near the boundaries of tectonic plates, and drilling deep wells is expensive and risky, since a well may fail to reach sufficient heat. In some cases, drilling has even been linked to earthquakes.

title: Yaşayan mirası korumak
text: When UNESCO adopted an international agreement to safeguard what it calls intangible cultural heritage, practices ranging from traditional crafts to oral storytelling were formally recognised as worthy of international support. Unlike monuments, such heritage survives only as long as people continue to practise it, which poses a distinctive dilemma for those trying to preserve it. Recording a dance or a festival on film may document its present form, yet it also threatens to freeze a tradition that has always evolved in response to changing social conditions. Inscription on international lists, bringing prestige and tourist money, can also tempt communities to perform their customs for visitors rather than for themselves, gradually altering their original meaning. Critics contend that effective safeguarding should focus less on fixing traditions in place and more on keeping alive the social contexts through which they are passed on.

title: Hatırlayarak öğrenmek
text: A large body of research in cognitive psychology shows that actively recalling information, rather than simply rereading it, yields more durable learning. Known as the testing effect, this finding has been replicated across age groups and subjects, from language learning to medical training. In a typical experiment of this kind, students who read a text once and then tried to recall it without looking outperformed, a week later, those who had read the same text several times, even though the latter group reported feeling more confident. This discrepancy suggests that learners frequently misjudge which strategies work best, mistaking the ease of rereading for genuine understanding. Despite such evidence, low-stakes quizzes remain underused in many classrooms, partly because teachers associate tests with grading rather than with learning itself.

title: Eriyen donmuş toprak
text: Permafrost, ground that remains frozen for years at a time, covers a large proportion of the land in the far north and is believed to store more carbon than is now present in the atmosphere. As Arctic temperatures climb considerably faster than the global average, this frozen soil is beginning to thaw, allowing microbes to decompose organic matter that had been locked away for thousands of years. The carbon dioxide and methane released in the process further warm the planet, which in turn accelerates thawing, creating what scientists call a feedback loop. Estimating the scale of this danger is difficult, though, because thawing is uneven: in some areas it proceeds gradually over decades, whereas abrupt collapses of ice-rich ground can expose deep layers far more quickly. For this reason, climate models that simulate only slow thaw may underestimate future emissions.

title: Algoritmalardaki önyargı
text: Machine-learning systems are often presented as neutral tools, yet their outputs can be no more impartial than the data from which they learn. When a facial recognition program is trained mostly on images of lighter-skinned men, for example, it tends to perform considerably worse on darker-skinned women, a disparity reported in several independent audits. Such errors are not just technical inconveniences: used in policing, hiring or lending decisions, a biased model can systematically disadvantage groups that are already under-represented, and at the same time give its judgments an air of scientific authority that makes them harder to question. Fixing the problem thus takes more than collecting larger datasets. Developers must also scrutinize how the data were gathered, test accuracy for each population on its own, and make the criteria behind automated decisions transparent to the people they concern.

title: Şehirlerde bisiklet yolları
text: Many cities around the world want to encourage people to cycle instead of driving. Cars cause traffic jams and air pollution, and they take up a lot of space. To deal with these problems, cities such as Copenhagen and Amsterdam have built wide bicycle lanes that are separated from the roads. As a result, cycling there is safe and fast. In Copenhagen, a large proportion of people travel to work or school by bike. Other cities have launched bike-sharing programmes. However, cycling requires good planning. If lanes are narrow or dangerous, few people will use them.

title: Vatandaş bilimi
text: Scientists cannot always collect all the data they need by themselves. For this reason, many research projects now rely on ordinary people. This approach is called citizen science. For instance, in some countries thousands of volunteers count the birds they see each year and send the numbers to researchers. These counts help scientists monitor changes in bird populations over many years. Other volunteers sort photos of distant galaxies on their home computers. Citizen science has clear benefits. It is cheap, and it gives scientists a vast amount of information. Moreover, the volunteers learn a lot about science while they help.

title: Aile sofrası
text: In many societies, families used to eat together every evening. Today, this habit is becoming less common. Long working hours, busy school timetables and television mean that family members often eat at different times or in different rooms. This matters because shared meals are not only about food. They give parents and children a chance to talk and to maintain close relationships. Some studies indicate that teenagers who often eat with their families tend to do better at school. They may also be less likely to have problems with alcohol. However, researchers point out that the quality of the conversation matters more than the meal itself.

title: Işık kirliliği
text: At night, most cities are full of bright lights from streets, buildings and cars. This light is essential for safety, but it also creates a problem called light pollution. Because of it, many people who live in cities can no longer see the Milky Way. Light pollution is harmful to animals, too. Many species of birds fly at night and become confused by city lights, so they sometimes hit tall buildings. Baby sea turtles sometimes move towards bright lights on the shore instead of the sea. Fortunately, this problem is easy to reduce. Cities can use lights that point downwards and switch them off when nobody needs them.

title: Uzun süre oturmanın riskleri
text: For most of human history, people spent much of the day on their feet, walking, farming or hunting. Today, many adults spend most of their waking hours sitting, whether at a desk, in a car or in front of a screen. Researchers have found that prolonged sitting is associated with a higher chance of heart disease, diabetes and obesity. Surprisingly, a short daily workout does not entirely remove this danger: a person who goes to the gym for an hour but then sits for the rest of the day may still be affected. Experts therefore suggest that office workers should stand up and move around regularly throughout the day. Some companies have also introduced standing desks, although evidence of their long-term benefits is still weak.

title: Erteleme alışkanlığı
text: Procrastination, the habit of delaying tasks that need to be done, is often regarded as a sign of laziness or poor time management. However, psychologists who have studied the behaviour suggest that it is largely an emotional problem rather than a practical one. People tend to postpone tasks that make them feel anxious, bored or unsure, and avoiding the task provides instant relief from these unpleasant feelings. Unfortunately, this relief is temporary, and the stress usually returns, often stronger than before, as the deadline approaches. For this reason, simply giving procrastinators a better schedule rarely solves the problem. Approaches that help people cope with negative emotions, such as breaking a task into smaller steps, tend to be more effective.

title: Mikrokredi
text: Microcredit refers to very small loans given to poor people who are unable to borrow from ordinary banks because they have no property or regular income. The idea became popular in the late twentieth century, when projects in South Asia began lending small sums to women so that they could start small businesses such as weaving or raising chickens. Supporters claimed that microcredit would help millions escape poverty, and the approach soon won international praise. However, later studies, which compared borrowers with similar people who had not received loans, produced more modest results. The loans enabled some families to manage emergencies and plan their spending, but they rarely led to a significant rise in income. Many economists now argue that credit alone cannot end poverty.

title: Su ayıları
text: Tardigrades, also known as water bears, are tiny animals, barely visible to the naked eye, that live in moss, soil and water. Although they look fragile, they are among the toughest organisms on Earth. When their environment dries out, tardigrades lose almost all the water in their bodies and shrink into a dry, barrel-shaped form, a state in which their metabolism virtually stops. In this condition, they can survive extreme cold, intense heat and, according to some experiments, even the conditions of outer space. Scientists have also identified special proteins that appear to protect their cells and DNA from damage. This discovery has attracted the interest of medical researchers, who hope they might one day help to preserve vaccines or human cells without refrigeration.

title: Matbaanın etkisi
text: Before the arrival of printing, books in Europe were copied by hand, a slow and expensive process that meant only churches, universities and rich families could own them. In the fifteenth century, Johannes Gutenberg developed a printing press that used movable metal letters, which could be arranged, inked and reused many times. Within a few decades, printing shops had spread to many European cities, and vast numbers of books had been produced. The consequences were enormous. Because books became cheaper, literacy slowly rose, and new ideas could circulate far more quickly than before. Historians point out, for instance, that the Protestant Reformation would hardly have spread so fast without printed pamphlets. Printing also helped to standardise languages, as printers tended to favour consistent spellings.

title: Genler ve ilaç yanıtı
text: Doctors have long observed that a drug which works well for one patient may prove ineffective, or even dangerous, for another receiving exactly the same dose. Much of this variation is now attributed to differences in the genes encoding the liver enzymes responsible for breaking down medicines. Individuals carrying certain variants metabolise some drugs so slowly that the compounds accumulate to toxic levels, whereas so-called ultra-rapid metabolisers may clear a medicine from the body before it has had time to work. Pharmacogenomics, the field examining these interactions, seeks to replace the traditional trial-and-error method of prescribing with treatment tailored to each patient's genetic profile. Although genetic testing has become far cheaper, its routine use remains rare, partly because many physicians lack training in interpreting the results and partly because proof of improved patient outcomes is still being gathered.

title: Verimlilik paradoksu
text: It seems self-evident that making appliances, cars and factories more energy-efficient should cut overall energy consumption. Yet as early as the nineteenth century, economists observed that improvements in the efficiency of steam engines had been accompanied not by a fall but by a rise in coal use. Because efficiency lowers the cost of each unit of useful energy, consumers and firms tend to use more of it, driving further, heating larger homes or expanding production. Many contemporary estimates suggest that this so-called rebound effect erodes only part of the expected savings, although its size varies widely from one sector to another. Its existence nevertheless implies that efficiency standards, unless they are accompanied by measures such as carbon pricing, may deliver smaller environmental gains than engineers predict.

title: Bağlam ve iletişim
text: Several decades ago, an influential anthropologist proposed a distinction between what he termed high-context and low-context cultures, a framework that continues to shape research on intercultural communication. In low-context societies, of which Germany and the United States are frequently cited as examples, meaning is expected to be conveyed explicitly through words, so a speaker who leaves important points unstated may be perceived as vague or evasive. In high-context societies such as Japan, by comparison, much of the message resides in shared understandings, tone and the relationship between the speakers, and spelling everything out can seem condescending. Critics contend that the model oversimplifies national cultures, which are far from uniform. Even so, many trainers believe that awareness of these differences can reduce misunderstandings in international business negotiations.

title: Tohum bankaları
text: As industrial agriculture has come to rely on a narrow range of high-yielding crop varieties, thousands of traditional strains that farmers cultivated for centuries have vanished from the fields. This loss of genetic diversity is more than a cultural concern: older varieties often carry traits, such as tolerance to drought or resistance to particular pests, that breeders may need as climate change exposes crops to unfamiliar stresses. To safeguard this heritage, governments and research institutes have established gene banks around the world, the best known being a large seed vault in the Arctic. Its value was demonstrated when researchers displaced by war withdrew duplicate samples from such a facility to rebuild collections they had been forced to leave behind. Seed banks are no cure-all, however, since stored seeds cannot evolve alongside the pests and diseases they will eventually face.

title: Ötegezegen avı
text: Over the past few decades, astronomers have catalogued thousands of planets orbiting other stars, known as exoplanets, many of them detected by the transit method. This technique exploits the slight but measurable dimming that occurs when a planet passes in front of its host star as seen from Earth; by monitoring the brightness of thousands of stars simultaneously, space telescopes have been able to identify periodic dips that signal orbiting bodies. The depth of each dip reveals the planet's size relative to its star, while the interval between transits indicates the length of its year. The method has an inherent bias, however: because a transit is visible only when a planet's orbit is aligned almost edge-on to our line of sight, the vast majority of planetary systems remain hidden from it.
